pool.name: CS Fundamentals — Software and Operating Systems
pool.description: 30 explained questions about software, operating systems, processes, scheduling, memory, files, drivers, permissions, application lifecycle, and introductory virtualization. Ten per difficulty, with six-question tests sampling two per level.

notes.title: 1. What Is Software?
notes.summary: Distinguish instructions from physical hardware and applications from system software.
notes.contentHtml:
Objective: explain how hardware becomes usable

Software consists of programs and related instructions and data that tell a computer what to do. Hardware is the physical equipment executing or supporting those instructions. A keyboard is hardware; a browser is software. The saved browser program occupies physical storage, but its instructions are not the same thing as the storage device.

Programs and instructions

A program describes operations. The CPU ultimately executes machine instructions, while software may be written in higher-level languages and translated or interpreted through other software. You do not need to program yet: the key idea is that the same hardware can perform different tasks by running different instructions.

Application software

Applications help users do tasks. Examples include browsers for web pages, editors for writing, games for play, and media players for sound and video. Different apps can work with the same saved file, provided they support its format and have permission to access it.

System software

System software manages the computing environment and supports applications. Operating systems, device drivers, and many system utilities belong here. The boundary can vary in everyday language, but the purpose is more useful than memorizing a label: does the software mainly support the system, or help the user complete a task?

How the two cooperate

When an editor saves a document, it usually requests file services from the OS. The OS manages the filesystem, access checks, and device communication. The editor need not implement a separate low-level storage controller for every drive. This cooperation makes many different applications practical on the same computer.

Practice

Classify a mouse, browser, SSD, operating system, game, and printer driver. Then explain why installing a new editor changes what the computer can do without replacing the keyboard or processor.

notes.title: 2. What Is an Operating System?
notes.summary: Understand familiar operating systems, interfaces, system services, and the OS's coordinating role.
notes.contentHtml:
The OS provides a managed environment

An operating system manages hardware resources and provides services that programs use. It helps applications share the CPU, memory, storage, and devices. Without these services, each application would need to handle far more low-level work itself, and sharing resources safely would be harder.

Examples

Windows, macOS, and Linux-based systems commonly run on personal computers and servers. Android and iOS are familiar mobile operating systems. Different devices and OS versions support different apps and interfaces. An application written for one system may need a compatible version or other support to run on another.

Interface and services

A desktop, application launcher, settings panel, or touch interface helps people interact with the system. These visible parts are not the entire OS. Much of its work happens out of sight: managing processes, providing file access, enforcing permissions, coordinating device input and output, and supporting networking.

A graphical interface uses windows, icons, menus, or touch controls. A command-line interface accepts typed commands. Both can request OS services. A system can offer both, and using a command line does not automatically grant administrator privileges.

Between applications and hardware

An app may ask to play sound through a system API. The OS and relevant drivers arrange hardware access. This is a useful management model, not a claim that every individual instruction must be interpreted by the OS. Ordinary application computations typically execute on the CPU, while privileged resource operations use controlled mechanisms.

Why this matters

A working screen and CPU alone do not provide a complete user environment. The OS coordinates the physical machine so apps can run, users can organize files, and shared resources can be controlled. Some simple embedded systems use specialized software without a full general-purpose OS; this topic focuses on familiar personal and mobile computers.

Practice

Name your device's OS without confusing it with the browser. Describe one visible interface feature and one background service you rely on when opening and saving a document.

notes.title: 3. How Operating Systems Manage Resources
notes.summary: Connect programs and processes to CPU scheduling, memory allocation, filesystems, and drivers.
notes.contentHtml:
A program is not the same as a process

A program is a set of instructions, often saved on storage. A process is a running instance with execution state and resources such as memory. Opening an app can create one or more processes. Browsers often use multiple processes, so the number of process rows is not necessarily the number of visible app windows.

CPU scheduling

The OS scheduler decides which runnable threads get CPU time. On one core, rapid switching lets several tasks make progress over time; multiple cores also permit suitable tasks to execute simultaneously. A waiting task may not need CPU time until data or input is ready. Responsive multitasking does not mean every task runs on every core at the same instant.

Memory allocation

The OS tracks memory use and helps provide each process with its working address space and protections. Apps request memory for code and data. The OS can use virtual memory and, where configured, storage-backed paging to handle demand. Storage-backed paging is not as fast as physical RAM. Heavy memory pressure may cause slowdowns, even if the drive has plenty of capacity.

Files and directories

A filesystem organizes saved data into files and directories and maintains information such as names and access rights. Apps normally use OS file operations to open, read, write, and close files. A directory is another term for a folder. RAM allocation and file saving are different operations: changing a document in memory does not automatically guarantee that the file has been updated.

Device drivers

A driver is software that helps the OS communicate with a device using its supported interface. Printing may involve an app, the OS print service, a driver, and the printer. A physical cable supplies a connection; a driver supplies communication support. Drivers should come from trusted system updates or verified manufacturers, not random download sites.

Practice

Imagine an editor and music player running together. Explain how scheduling shares CPU time, memory holds their working data, file services retrieve saved content, and drivers help send audio or printer output. Do not assume that one busy process identifies every possible bottleneck.

notes.title: 4. Files, Permissions, and Users
notes.summary: Understand accounts, least privilege, read/write/execute access, and graphical versus command-line interfaces.
notes.contentHtml:
Accounts give actions an identity

A user account identifies a person or service and helps the OS apply settings and access rules. A standard account is intended for ordinary work. An administrator can authorize system-wide changes, but should not be treated as permission to bypass every safety boundary. Some protections still apply, and elevated access can cause greater damage if misused.

Read, write, and execute

  • Read: access a file's contents.
  • Write: change data, subject to the system's rules.
  • Execute: run a program where that permission model applies.

Permission models vary across operating systems. Directories can have additional meanings for these rights; deleting or renaming files may depend on directory permissions, not only a file's write flag. For now, understand the intended action and check the system's actual rules rather than assuming that read access grants every action.

Application access

Apps may also face sandbox rules and explicit consent for sensitive data or devices, such as photos, a microphone, or a camera. A signed-in user being able to view something does not always mean every app automatically receives access. Limiting access protects data and reduces the effect of mistakes or malicious software.

Least privilege

Grant only the access needed for the task. If an editor cannot save into a protected system folder, choose an authorized document location or ask the administrator. Do not disable protections or grant broad access simply to finish a practice task. Unexpected permission requests should be investigated.

Graphical and command-line interfaces

A file manager uses visual controls; a shell accepts typed commands. Both operate within account privileges and other security rules. A command line is not inherently unsafe or all-powerful, but unfamiliar commands can have serious effects. This lesson does not require entering administrator commands or changing permissions.

Practice

A shared report should be readable but not edited by classmates. Explain why read-only access is useful, which permission an authorized editor needs, and why everyone should not be given administrator privileges.

notes.title: 5. Application Lifecycle
notes.summary: Follow installation, launch, execution, closing, freezes, updates, and background startup behavior.
notes.contentHtml:
From installation to closing

  1. Install: place application files and required configuration on the system using an approved source and method.
  2. Launch: request that the OS start the application; needed code and resources become available to one or more processes.
  3. Run: the app responds to input, performs work, and uses resources.
  4. Close or quit: request normal termination so the app can prompt to save work and release resources. Closing a window may not quit the entire app on every system.

An installed app is not necessarily running. A running background process may have no visible window. Some applications start automatically at sign-in to sync files or provide services; others are optional convenience tools.

When an app freezes

A frozen app may stop responding because it is busy, waiting, or affected by a fault. A brief Not responding indicator is not proof of a permanent failure. First wait reasonably and check whether the rest of the system responds. If possible, save work in other apps. Try the application's normal close action before considering forced termination.

Task Manager on Windows or Force Quit and Activity Monitor on macOS can help inspect or end an unresponsive app. Force quitting can lose unsaved work and should be a last resort for the identified app. Do not terminate unknown system processes or other people's work. Restarting the entire computer can affect more tasks than closing one app.

Updates and startup apps

Trusted updates may fix bugs and security weaknesses. Save work before a required restart and use system or verified publisher update mechanisms. An update changes stored software; it is not the same as merely launching the existing version. Some updates restart background services.

Startup apps consume resources even before you open their windows. Review only settings you understand and have permission to change. Do not disable security tools or system services to make a usage graph look smaller. Low free memory or high CPU usage is evidence to interpret, not a reason to close random processes.

Practice

Explain the difference between installed, running, minimized, and closed. Describe a cautious recovery plan for an unresponsive editor and identify where unsaved work may be at risk.

notes.title: 6. Virtualization — An Introduction
notes.summary: Explain virtual machines, hosts, guests, shared physical resources, and developer use cases.
notes.contentHtml:
A software-managed computer inside a physical computer

A virtual machine (VM) presents a virtual computer environment that can run its own guest operating system. A virtualization layer, often called a hypervisor, manages virtual CPU, memory, storage, and devices using real physical resources. The physical system is the host; the OS inside the VM is the guest.

Virtual hardware is not an extra physical processor magically created inside the case. Guest work still requires the host's CPU time, RAM, and storage. Configuring virtual resources does not manufacture more physical capacity. Virtual disks are commonly represented by files or allocated storage on the host.

Why developers use VMs

  • Test software on another operating system or version.
  • Keep a repeatable development environment separate from everyday work.
  • Practice system administration without changing the primary installation.
  • Use snapshots, where supported, to return guest state to an earlier point after experiments.

Physical versus virtual

A physical computer has real components. A virtual computer exposes managed representations of components to its guest. Both can run programs and maintain files, but the VM depends on a suitable host and virtualization support. Assigning too much RAM or too many active workloads can slow both guest and host.

Useful isolation, not an absolute guarantee

VMs help separate environments, but shared folders, networking, clipboard integration, software vulnerabilities, and configuration affect isolation. A snapshot is not necessarily an independent backup of every host and guest file. Do not experiment with untrusted software or assume a VM removes all risk.

You do not need to install or create a VM for this introduction. Virtualization support, licensing, image downloads, and organization policy need review before setup.

Practice

A developer wants to test a Linux app while retaining their main desktop OS. Explain how a guest VM could help, name the real resources it needs, and give one reason to leave enough memory for the host.

notes.title: 7. Practical Activity — Observe Computer Resources
notes.summary: Safely inspect processes and resource usage, distinguish storage capacity from activity, and explain observations.
notes.contentHtml:
Observe first; do not change the system

Use a computer you are allowed to inspect. Open Task Manager on Windows through the Start menu or Ctrl+Shift+Esc, or Activity Monitor on macOS from Applications/Utilities or search. Linux users can use an available system monitor. Names, tabs, permissions, and CPU percentage conventions differ by system version.

Guided observation

  1. Identify a familiar app, such as your editor or browser, in the process list. A browser may have several processes; record that rather than assuming each is a separate visible window.
  2. Open a small practice text document in your own editor. Observe whether a new process appears or an existing app handles the window.
  3. Locate CPU usage. Watch for a short period: values fluctuate. A high value can reflect useful work, and a single sample does not prove a problem.
  4. Locate memory use. Identify the units and note that the OS, services, and apps all consume memory. Do not add or compare figures blindly when the tool labels them differently.
  5. Inspect storage activity using Task Manager's disk view or Activity Monitor's Disk tab. This measures operations or data movement, not necessarily remaining capacity.
  6. Check free storage separately through File Explorer's This PC/properties on Windows or System Settings/General/Storage or Finder disk information on macOS, where available. Do not confuse read/write activity with GB of free space.
  7. Save and close your practice document normally. Observe which windows or processes remain. Do not force quit anything for this exercise.

Write a short resource report

Record the OS, one recognizable application, its process name or names, observed CPU and memory readings with units, disk activity, and available storage. Measurements are snapshots, not fixed properties. Avoid sharing screenshots containing usernames, sensitive file paths, or private application names.

Interpret a fictional example

An editor uses little CPU while waiting for typing, a video export uses substantial CPU, and the disk graph briefly rises when a large file is saved. These patterns can be normal. If many apps produce sustained memory pressure and paging, memory demand may be a limit even when 100 GB of disk space is free. Free disk capacity does not equal free RAM.

Safety and troubleshooting

If inspection is restricted, use this fictional example instead of bypassing restrictions. Do not end unknown processes, install monitor tools, disable startup services, change permissions, or elevate privileges for the activity. If a genuine app freeze occurs, follow the cautious recovery steps in the lifecycle lesson and remember that force quitting can lose unsaved changes.

Completion checklist

  • I can distinguish hardware, applications, and system software.
  • I can explain why an OS manages CPU, memory, files, and devices.
  • I can distinguish a saved program from a running process.
  • I can explain read, write, and execute access and least privilege.
  • I can describe the application lifecycle and safe freeze recovery.
  • I can explain host and guest VMs and their physical resource needs.
  • I can interpret basic CPU, memory, and disk observations without confusing activity with capacity.

Completion outcome

You understand why an OS exists and how software uses computer resources. Explain how an editor can receive input, update memory, and save a file while another app plays music. The test draws two easy, two medium, and two hard questions from this topic's separate 30-question pool.

questions.questionText: Which example is software rather than hardware?
options: A physical keyboard
A metal computer case
A web browser application
A power cable
questions.explanation: A browser is a program. A keyboard, case, and cable are physical hardware.

questions.questionText: What is a primary purpose of an operating system?
options: Manage resources and provide services to applications
Replace the need for all hardware
Guarantee every website is truthful
Physically cool the room
questions.explanation: The OS manages resources such as CPU time, memory, files, and devices while supporting applications.

questions.questionText: Which item is an operating system?
options: A USB cable
A photo named holiday.jpg
A keyboard shortcut
Android
questions.explanation: Android is an operating system commonly used on mobile devices. The other choices are not operating systems.

questions.questionText: Which is an example of application software?
options: A RAM chip
A text editor
A display cable
A battery
questions.explanation: A text editor helps a user perform a task and is application software. The other choices are hardware.

questions.questionText: What is a process?
options: Only a filename extension
A type of screen connector
A running instance of a program with execution state and resources
An unopened folder on a shelf
questions.explanation: A process is a running program instance with execution state and resources, not just the saved program file.

questions.questionText: What does a device driver help the operating system do?
options: Communicate with a hardware device
Choose a user's favorite game
Create electrical power from nothing
Turn every file into an image
questions.explanation: Drivers support communication between the OS and devices using their interfaces.

questions.questionText: What does read permission generally allow for a file?
options: Automatically delete every folder
Change all system settings
Run every program as administrator
Access the file's contents
questions.explanation: Read permission generally allows accessing contents, not unrestricted editing, deletion, or administrative actions.

questions.questionText: What is a command-line interface?
options: A physical storage drive
An interface that accepts typed commands
Only an image of a keyboard
A computer without any software
questions.explanation: A command-line interface uses typed commands to request actions. It can coexist with graphical interfaces.

questions.questionText: Which Windows tool can show running processes and resource usage?
options: A speaker volume knob
A USB hub
Task Manager
A blank text file
questions.explanation: Task Manager shows processes and resource information. Activity Monitor serves a comparable role on macOS.

questions.questionText: What is a virtual machine in this topic?
options: A software-managed computer environment capable of running a guest OS
A second physical computer automatically created by renaming a folder
Only a browser bookmark
A battery that never needs charging
questions.explanation: A VM exposes virtual hardware managed by a virtualization layer and uses resources from a physical host.

questions.questionText: An editor is installed on storage but has not been launched. Which statement is correct?
options: It must already be using a full CPU core
Its window must be visible
It no longer exists as software
Its program files can be present without an active editor process
questions.explanation: Installation places saved software on the system. Launching starts execution; installed and running are different states.

questions.questionText: How can one CPU core let several apps make progress over time?
options: By storing all instructions in the monitor
By scheduling runnable work and switching between tasks
By removing the operating system
By making every task run simultaneously on that single core
questions.explanation: Scheduling and switching share a core's time. Concurrency over time does not require all tasks to execute simultaneously on one core.

questions.questionText: A shared report should be viewable but not edited by classmates. Which access is most appropriate?
options: Administrator access for everyone
Unrestricted write access for everyone
Read access without unnecessary write access
No permissions because filenames enforce security
questions.explanation: Read-only access supports viewing while limiting modification, following the principle of least privilege.

questions.questionText: A printer is connected, but the OS lacks compatible device communication support. Which software may be needed?
options: A trusted compatible printer driver
A randomly renamed photograph
A larger wallpaper image
A new text document
questions.explanation: A compatible driver helps the OS communicate with the printer. Obtain it through trusted OS or manufacturer channels.

questions.questionText: Why might an application be unable to access the microphone even when the user is signed in?
options: Every signed-in app automatically has unlimited device access
Microphones are always output devices
Only apps with no windows can use microphones
OS privacy or sandbox rules may require separate permission
questions.explanation: User identity does not automatically grant every app access to sensitive devices. The OS can impose consent and sandbox restrictions.

questions.questionText: You see several processes for one browser. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: Every process must be a separate physical computer
The browser may use multiple processes for its work
The process list cannot be correct
Each row always means one visible app window
questions.explanation: One application can use several processes, including background and support processes, so rows need not correspond to windows.

questions.questionText: What is a suitable first response when an editor briefly stops responding?
options: Immediately unplug the computer
Terminate every process in the list
Wait reasonably, check whether other apps respond, and try normal recovery before forcing it to quit
Disable all account permissions
questions.explanation: Temporary busyness is possible. A cautious response avoids unnecessary forced termination and loss of unsaved work.

questions.questionText: Why do developers use virtual machines?
options: To test another OS or maintain a separate, repeatable environment
To obtain unlimited physical RAM for free
To eliminate all security risks automatically
To avoid using a real processor
questions.explanation: VMs support separate testing environments, but still consume real host resources and require appropriate security measures.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly compares graphical and command-line interfaces?
options: A command line always bypasses access restrictions
Graphical interfaces cannot use files
Only command lines can run programs
Both can request OS actions and remain subject to privileges and security rules
questions.explanation: The interface style does not itself grant authority. Account privileges and other protections apply to actions requested through either interface.

questions.questionText: Which statement about background and startup applications is correct?
options: Anything without a visible window uses no resources
Some software runs at sign-in or in the background without a visible window
Every startup app is malicious
All background services should always be disabled
questions.explanation: Background and startup software can provide useful services and consume resources. Changes should be authorized and based on understanding.

questions.questionText: A learner sees low free RAM and frequent paging but 100 GB of free disk capacity. Why can the computer still be slow?
options: Free storage automatically makes RAM unlimited
Folders prevent the CPU from working
Working-memory pressure can cause slower storage-backed paging despite ample file space
An operating system never uses memory
questions.explanation: Free disk capacity and available RAM are different resources. Paging can help memory management but is generally slower than RAM access.

questions.questionText: A user can read a shared file but cannot save edits to it. Which response best follows least privilege?
options: Use an authorized writable location or request the specific needed access from the owner
Grant every user administrator rights
Disable all OS access controls
Try random administrator commands from an unknown page
questions.explanation: A legitimate workflow should use permitted locations or request narrowly scoped access, rather than broadly bypassing protections.

questions.questionText: A video export briefly uses high CPU while the editor is responsive. What can be concluded from this single observation?
options: The CPU must be broken
The application must be malicious
Every other process should be forcibly ended
The export may be doing legitimate work; more context and observations are needed to diagnose a problem
questions.explanation: High utilization can be normal for computation-intensive work. A single reading does not prove a fault or justify terminating processes.

questions.questionText: An editor is persistently frozen, but other apps respond. Why is force quitting only the identified editor preferable to immediately restarting the whole computer?
options: Force quitting guarantees all unsaved text is preserved
It limits disruption to other work, although unsaved editor changes may still be lost
A restart can never affect other apps
Closing an app permanently deletes its installation
questions.explanation: Targeted recovery can reduce collateral disruption. Normal closure is preferred, and forced termination can still lose unsaved data.

questions.questionText: A developer assigns almost all host RAM to a guest VM and then both environments become sluggish. Which explanation is best?
options: Virtual RAM is independent of real hardware
The guest's wallpaper uses every CPU core
Host and guest compete for finite physical resources, so leaving sufficient host memory matters
Creating a VM always doubles physical memory
questions.explanation: Virtual resource allocations rely on physical host capacity. Excessive allocation or active demand can cause memory pressure and paging.

questions.questionText: Activity Monitor's Disk tab shows bytes read and written. Does that alone tell you the remaining free storage capacity?
options: No; disk activity measures data movement, while capacity must be checked through storage or disk information
Yes; bytes written always equal free space
Yes; CPU usage is also the same as free disk space
No, because computers never report free space
questions.explanation: Activity and available space measure different things. Use appropriate storage information to determine remaining capacity.

questions.questionText: A classmate says a VM is completely safe for any unknown software because it is isolated. What is the best correction?
options: VMs have no networking under any circumstances
A snapshot is always an independent backup of every host file
Guest software never uses real resources
Isolation depends on configuration and vulnerabilities; shared folders, networking, and integration can expose data
questions.explanation: VM isolation is useful but not absolute. Configuration, integration features, and security flaws affect risk; snapshots are not universal backups.

questions.questionText: A music player continues playing while an editor saves a document. Which explanation best connects OS responsibilities?
options: Only the monitor is working
Scheduling shares CPU time, memory supports active work, file services manage saving, and drivers support devices
The editor physically becomes a speaker
The OS must stop every other task whenever a file is saved
questions.explanation: The OS coordinates multiple resources and services so apps can make progress together; no single component handles all these roles.

questions.questionText: A user installs an update and then launches the app. Which distinction is correct?
options: Launching always installs a new version
Installing and running are identical states
Updating changes stored software, while launching starts execution of an available version
An app cannot run after any update
questions.explanation: Updating modifies the installed software; launching starts its execution. Some update workflows also restart apps or services, but the concepts differ.

questions.questionText: A process list shows an unfamiliar system service using memory. What is the safest approach during this observation exercise?
options: Observe and identify its purpose through trusted information without terminating it or changing privileges
End it immediately because unfamiliar means malicious
Disable every service with no window
Install an unknown cleanup utility and grant administrator access
questions.explanation: System services can be necessary and legitimately consume resources. Observation should not become unauthorized or uninformed modification of the system.
